catalog_quote: 2.3 STRESS. Stress is assigned as follows: (1) if the first syllable involves a long vowel, then it must receive primary stress; (2) if there is no long vowel in a word, and (a) the word is disyllabic or quadrisyllabic, primary stress goes on the first syllable; (b) the word is trisyllabic or quinquesyllabic, primary stress goes on the second syllable. Secondary stress goes on the syllable next but one after primary stress, except that a final syllable can never bear stress. Thus: (1) mú:ba 'stone fish', gí:baɽa 'fig tree'; (2)(a) báda 'dog' ...; (b) gagáɽa 'dilly bag', guɽágay-mìri 'Niagara Vale-FROM'. It will be seen that stress shifts between the absolutive form of a noun (which involves zero inflection) and an oblique form, e.g. múŋan 'mountain-ABS' muŋán-da 'mountain-LOC'. The Wargamay stress assignment rules make it impossible to get two successive stressed syllables ... A non-ini…
sweep_summary: One item in the sweep: Kager 1995 'On foot templates and root templates' (Linguistics in the Netherlands 12). It is open access (CC BY-NC) on the Benjamins platform; fetched sources, text-extracted, and the Wargamay page (p. 130) checked on the page image, with a line. Section 3 restates Dixon 1981's Wargamay stress rule with Dixon's examples (heavy initial syllable stressed; else initial in even-syllabled words, second in odd-syllabled words, slightly lengthened; secondary stress non-final, no clash) and reanalyses it as bimoraic [H]/[LL] feet with a mixed trochaic/iambic parse; its data are entirely from Dixon 1981 (one citation 'Dixon 1983:20' is a slip for Dixon 1981:20). It confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding and does not supersede Dixon 1981 as the deciding source. Nothing left to acquire from this sweep. web lookups on DOI/Crossref/OpenAlex and a direct download were used instead.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Wargamay falls on a heavy syllable (11a-c), and in words that have no heavy syllables, on the initial syllable in even-numbered words (11d, f) and on the second syllable in odd-numbered words (11e, g), which is slightly lengthened. Secondary stress goes on the penult, but no clash is allowed: (11) a yáa 'top of tree' b múuba 'stone fish' c gíibaɽa 'fig tree' d báda 'dog' e gagáˑra 'dilly bag' f gídawùlu 'freshwater jewfish' g ɟuɽáˑgay-mìri 'Niagara Vale - FROM'

new_statements.reading: Secondary, not first-hand: Kager restates Dixon 1981's rule (initial long vowel = heavy syllable takes primary stress; otherwise 1st syllable in 2/4-syllable words, 2nd syllable in 3/5-syllable words; secondary stress non-final, no clash) and reanalyses it as a bimoraic [H]/[LL] foot with a mixed trochaic/iambic parse. It matches the catalog's 'weight' coding (initial CVV heavy, parity-dependent default otherwise) exactly, and adds the observation that the non-initial stressed vowel in odd-syllabled words is slightly lengthened (also in Dixon). Because it contains no new field data it does not supersede Dixon 1981, which remains the deciding source.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated locator in the held ANU scan (pdf pp.44-45 = printed pp.20-21, sec. 2.3), and the ch.1 restatement at pdf p.25 is also present. Deciding source: Dixon 1981 is a 144-page reference grammar with an explicit stress section, written by the only linguist to document the language from its last speakers; Glottolog lists no competing grammar, phonology or instrumental study, and the later Dixon 2015 volume (TOC checked at OUP) treats Warrgamay morphosyntax, not stress. Secondary treatments (Hayes 1995, Bailey 1995, McGarrity 2003, StressTyp2) all derive from Dixon 1981; the noted StressTyp2 partial mismatch is a reanalysis artefact, not a source conflict.
